title: Nvidia in Talks to Invest $3 Billion in SB Energy as Part of Massive OpenAI Data Center Deal
excerpt: The chipmaker is negotiating a multibillion-dollar stake in SoftBank's energy subsidiary alongside roughly $100 billion in credit support for a 10-gigawatt Ohio data center that could become the largest ever built.
body:
• Nvidia is in talks to invest up to $3 billion in SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary developing what would be the world's largest data center complex in Ohio.
  • The chipmaker is also negotiating roughly $100 billion in credit support for the project's first phase, downsized from an original $250 billion guarantee that rattled Nvidia's stock.
  • OpenAI is still in discussions to sign a binding lease for the full 10-gigawatt facility, which could cost over $500 billion including chips.
  • A deal could be signed as soon as this weekend, with Goldman Sachs advising SB Energy and Morgan Stanley advising Nvidia.

Nvidia is negotiating an investment of up to $3 billion in SB Energy, the SoftBank subsidiary at the center of what could become the largest data center project ever attempted, according to Reuters. The equity stake is part of a broader package that would see the chipmaker provide approximately $100 billion in credit guarantees for a massive AI computing facility in Ohio.

The project, which SB Energy is developing to support OpenAI's infrastructure needs, envisions a 10-gigawatt campus — a scale that dwarfs anything currently operational. At full buildout, the total cost could exceed $500 billion, including the Nvidia chips that would fill it.

A Deal Scaled Back From Its Original Ambitions

The negotiations have already undergone significant revision. Nvidia's original guarantee was reported at $250 billion — a figure that prompted a 5% drop in Nvidia's share price as investors questioned the risk exposure. The current discussions involve less than $120 billion for the first phase, targeting roughly 5 gigawatts of capacity, the Wall Street Journal reported.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=CF7Z52FEEZk

The $3 billion equity investment in SB Energy would give Nvidia a direct financial stake in the project's success beyond its role as the primary chip supplier. Goldman Sachs is advising SB Energy on the transaction, while Morgan Stanley is representing Nvidia.

"Vendor financing like this usually don't end well."

— Jay Goldberg, analyst at Seaport Research Partners

OpenAI, valued at $852 billion despite remaining unprofitable, is still negotiating a binding lease for the full 10-gigawatt facility. Without that commitment, the project's later phases remain uncertain.

The Financing Architecture

The deal sits within a web of overlapping financial arrangements. Nvidia is separately discussing a deal to finance OpenAI's chip purchases worth up to $350 billion — effectively lending its biggest customer the money to buy its products.

Last week, Nvidia announced partnerships with Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to create "compute financing platforms" backed by more than $500 billion in outside capital. The strategy amounts to building a financial ecosystem around AI infrastructure, with Nvidia at its center.

Japan is contributing to the project's power supply under a recent trade deal, funding a $33 billion natural gas plant. The U.S. government controls power allocation for the site, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick involved in the process.

Echoes of the Telecom Bubble

Not everyone is convinced the model is sound. Seaport Research analyst Jay Goldberg has drawn parallels to Lucent Technologies, which extended vendor financing to telecom companies in the late 1990s — underwriting customers to buy its own equipment. When those customers collapsed, Lucent absorbed devastating losses.

The comparison is imperfect — the AI infrastructure buildout has backing from some of the world's largest asset managers, not just startup telecom carriers — but the structural dynamic is similar. Nvidia is deepening its financial entanglement with the very customers driving its revenue.

The original memorandum of understanding between Nvidia and OpenAI, signed last September for a 10-gigawatt, $100 billion investment, had already stalled over internal doubts before the current round of negotiations began.

What to Watch

A deal could be signed as soon as this weekend, according to people familiar with the negotiations. The key variables remain whether OpenAI commits to a binding lease for the full facility, how much credit risk Nvidia's board will ultimately accept, and whether the project can secure the power infrastructure a 10-gigawatt campus requires. For investors, the question is straightforward: is Nvidia building the backbone of a transformative technology cycle, or financing its own demand?
